questions.stem: A 24-year-old pregnant client at 14 weeks’ gestation has a low income, a hemoglobin of 10.2 g/dL, and says she often skips meals to make sure her 2-year-old eats. Which program referral best addresses her nutritional need?
options: Supplemental Security Income (SSI)
Indian Health Service (IHS) clinics
Medicaid pregnancy health coverage
Women, Infants, and Children (WIC)
optionRationales: Incorrect. SSI involves low income, but it is cash aid for people who are aged, blind, or disabled.
Incorrect. IHS provides health care for American Indian and Alaska Native people, and it is not a nutrition program.
Incorrect. Medicaid covers prenatal care and may treat her anemia, but it does not supply food for her or her toddler.
Correct. WIC provides supplemental food and nutrition education for pregnant women and children under 5 at nutritional risk.
questions.rationale: WIC is a supplemental nutrition program for pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women, infants, and children under age 5 who are at nutritional risk. This client is pregnant, anemic, food-insecure, and has a toddler, so both she and her child may qualify. WIC is typically accessed through local social services or local health department offices. SSI is tempting because it involves low income, but it is cash aid for aged, blind, or disabled people.
questions.takeaway: Pregnant women and children under 5 at nutritional risk → WIC.
questions.hintContent: Look for the program designed around pregnancy, early childhood, and nutrition risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Match the client’s defining characteristics (pregnancy, child under 5, nutrition) to the program’s eligibility rules.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Agencies & Accreditation · pp. 2799
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A hospital is preparing for its Joint Commission survey. Which actions by staff nurses reflect the nurse’s role in accreditation? Select all that apply.
options: Helping revise the unit’s pressure injury prevention policy using current evidence
Participating in a mock survey and chart audit on the unit
Explaining unit practices directly to surveyors during a tracer
Delaying entry of incident reports until after the survey ends
Referring every surveyor question to the nurse manager
optionRationales: Correct. Developing and revising evidence-based policies is part of the nurse’s role.
Correct. Organizational self-reviews such as mock surveys and audits are part of the nurse’s role.
Correct. Nurses speak directly with survey teams at the point of care.
Incorrect. Concealing or delaying event reports endangers clients and violates reporting expectations.
Incorrect. Surveyors expect frontline staff to answer about their own practice.
questions.rationale: The nurse’s role in Joint Commission accreditation includes developing and revising evidence-based policies, participating in organizational self-reviews, and speaking directly with survey teams at the point of care. Accreditation is about continuous quality, not presenting a perfect picture on survey day, so concealing events defeats its purpose and harms safety culture. Deferring every question to the manager suggests staff do not understand their own practice.
questions.takeaway: Nurses build evidence-based policies, join self-reviews, and talk with surveyors — they never hide events.
questions.hintContent: Accreditation reflects everyday quality, not survey-day appearances.
questions.hintStrategy: Select actions that show transparency and engagement; reject anything that hides information or avoids responsibility.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Agencies & Accreditation · pp. 2800–2801
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: While discarding a used needle from a syringe that lacks a safety feature, a nurse sustains a puncture wound to the finger. The client has a history of hepatitis C. What should the nurse do first?
options: Complete an incident report describing the device that caused the injury.
Notify employee health to arrange post-exposure testing and follow-up.
Wash the puncture site thoroughly with soap and water.
Ask the client for consent to test for bloodborne pathogens.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reporting is required, but it follows immediate first aid.
Incorrect. Prompt post-exposure evaluation is essential, but it follows immediate first aid.
Correct. Immediate washing of the site with soap and water is the first step after a percutaneous exposure.
Incorrect. Source testing is arranged through the post-exposure process after first aid, per facility protocol.
questions.rationale: After a needlestick, the first action is to wash the site with soap and water; then the nurse reports immediately to the supervisor and employee health for post-exposure evaluation and follow-up, and completes an incident report. OSHA’s bloodborne pathogens standard requires employers to provide safety-engineered devices, sharps containers, an exposure control plan, and post-exposure evaluation, so the unsafe device should also be reported through the safety process. Reporting options are tempting because they are required, but first aid comes first.
questions.takeaway: Needlestick: wash first, then report and get post-exposure evaluation; report unsafe devices.
questions.hintContent: Think about what reduces the risk to the nurse in the first minute after the injury.
questions.hintStrategy: When every option is eventually correct, put them in time order and choose the immediate physical action.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Agencies & Accreditation · pp. 2798–2799
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: During a Joint Commission tracer, a nurse hangs an IV antibiotic and then realizes she did not check the client’s two identifiers before starting the infusion. The surveyor is watching. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stop the infusion and verify the client’s identity with two identifiers.
Notify the provider of a possible medication error involving the antibiotic.
Assess the client for signs of a reaction to the IV antibiotic.
Complete an incident report describing the missed identity check.
optionRationales: Correct. Stopping the drug and confirming identity tells the nurse right away whether an error occurred and limits any harm.
Incorrect. The provider may need to be told, but the nurse first stops the infusion and confirms whether a wrong-client error happened.
Incorrect. Assessment follows, but the drug is still running; stopping it and verifying identity comes first.
Incorrect. Reporting the near miss is required, but it is done after the client is safe, not first.
questions.rationale: Using at least two client identifiers before giving medications is a core Joint Commission safety requirement. When the nurse recognizes an omission while the medication is infusing, the first action is to stop the infusion and verify identity, then assess the client, notify the provider if an error occurred, and report through the event-reporting system. Accreditation exists to protect clients, so the surveyor’s presence should not change the priority. Notifying the provider is tempting, but the nurse must first stop the drug and confirm whether an error actually occurred.
questions.takeaway: Client safety comes before survey appearances; stop and verify identity with two identifiers.
questions.hintContent: Which option directly removes the risk to the client right now?
questions.hintStrategy: Ignore the distraction in the stem (the surveyor) and apply standard safety priorities.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Agencies & Accreditation · pp. 2800–2801
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A client who stays at a homeless shelter comes to a free clinic with a 5-week productive cough, night sweats, weight loss, and blood-streaked sputum. He is sitting in the crowded waiting room. What should the nurse do first?
options: Collect a sputum specimen for acid-fast bacilli before he leaves the clinic.
Call the local health department to begin contact tracing at the shelter.
Ask the client to list everyone he has been in close contact with recently.
Give the client a surgical mask and move him to a separate room.
optionRationales: Incorrect. A sputum specimen is likely needed, but source control in the waiting room comes first.
Incorrect. Public health notification and contact tracing are needed after the provider evaluates the client, not before protecting people in the room.
Incorrect. A contact list helps public health later but does not reduce current exposure.
Correct. Masking and separating a client with possible active TB immediately reduces airborne transmission to others.
questions.rationale: Prolonged cough, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis in a congregate-living client strongly suggest active pulmonary TB, which spreads by the airborne route. The first priority is source control: place a surgical mask on the client and move him away from others, ideally to an airborne-infection isolation room, with staff wearing N95 respirators. Specimen collection, provider evaluation, reportable-disease notification, and contact tracing by the health department follow. Calling the health department is tempting because TB is reportable, but protecting the people in the waiting room comes first.
questions.takeaway: Suspected active TB: mask and separate the client first, then evaluate and report.
questions.hintContent: Who is at risk right now, and how is TB transmitted?
questions.hintStrategy: For infection-control priority items, choose the action that stops transmission immediately.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Agencies & Accreditation · pp. 2799
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A client enrolled in an HMO calls the clinic nurse while shopping. She reports that her husband suddenly has a drooping face, slurred speech, and weakness in his right arm. She asks whether she needs to call his primary care provider for a referral before taking him to a hospital. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: “Call his primary care provider first so the hospital visit will be covered.”
“Call 911 now; emergency care does not require a referral from his provider.”
“Drive him to the hospital in your HMO network, even if it is farther away.”
“Drive him to the nearest emergency department yourself right away.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. HMOs use the PCP as gatekeeper for routine care, but emergencies need no referral, and calling first delays stroke care.
Correct. Possible stroke is time-critical; EMS starts care, notifies a stroke center, and emergency care is covered without referral.
Incorrect. It respects the plan’s network, but emergency care is covered anywhere, and the longer drive delays treatment.
Incorrect. Going to the nearest ED is better, but driving loses EMS care en route and pre-arrival stroke alert.
questions.rationale: Sudden facial droop, slurred speech, and unilateral arm weakness indicate a possible stroke, a time-critical emergency. HMOs restrict nonemergency care to network providers and use the PCP as gatekeeper, but emergency care is covered without referral, and plans must cover emergency services without prior authorization. Insurance rules never justify delaying emergency care. The in-network hospital option is tempting because it seems to respect the plan, but it delays treatment and skips EMS.
questions.takeaway: Emergency care is never delayed for referrals or network rules.
questions.hintContent: Identify the clinical emergency first; then remember how HMOs handle emergencies.
questions.hintStrategy: When a stem mixes insurance details with an emergency, physical safety comes first and the insurance details are distractors.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2802–2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with an HMO plan noticed a changing mole on her back and asks the nurse how to get an appointment with a dermatologist. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Schedule with any dermatologist you choose; your plan will reimburse you.”
“Ask your primary care provider for a referral to an in-network dermatologist.”
“Your HMO does not cover specialist care, so you will need to pay out of pocket.”
“Show the mole to your primary care provider at your next annual checkup.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Many plans allow direct specialist visits, but an HMO limits coverage to network providers with a referral.
Correct. The HMO PCP acts as gatekeeper, and a changing mole needs prompt evaluation, so she asks the PCP for a referral now.
Incorrect. HMOs are restrictive, but they cover in-network specialists when the PCP refers the member.
Incorrect. The PCP is the right starting point, but a changing mole should be evaluated promptly, not at a routine yearly visit.
questions.rationale: An HMO is the most restrictive managed-care plan: coverage is limited to contracted network providers except in emergencies, and members usually select a primary care provider who acts as gatekeeper for referrals. A changing mole warrants timely evaluation, so the nurse explains the referral process and encourages the client to call the PCP promptly. The statement that HMOs do not cover specialists is tempting because HMOs are restrictive, but they do cover in-network specialists with referral.
questions.takeaway: HMO members reach in-network specialists through a PCP referral.
questions.hintContent: Recall the role of the primary care provider in an HMO.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the plan type’s defining rule before choosing; the answer usually applies that rule directly.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: The adult daughter of an 82-year-old client with advancing dementia says, “Dad can’t bathe or dress himself anymore. Medicare will pay for him to live in a nursing home permanently, right?” Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: “Yes. Medicare Part A covers nursing home care once a client needs help with daily activities.”
“Only a Medigap policy pays for permanent nursing home care, so you should buy one now.”
“Medicare Part B will cover the nursing home if his provider writes a prescription for it.”
“Medicare pays for short-term skilled care, not long-term custodial care. Let’s involve the social worker.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care such as help with bathing and dressing.
Incorrect. Medigap fills Original Medicare’s cost-sharing gaps; it does not add long-term custodial care.
Incorrect. Part B covers outpatient and provider services and DME, not custodial nursing home care.
Correct. It corrects the misconception accurately and refers the family to the social worker for options such as Medicaid or private resources.
questions.rationale: Medicare does not cover long-term care, routine dental or eye care, hearing aids, or cosmetic surgery. Part A covers only short-term skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, not ongoing custodial help with activities of daily living. Medicaid is the major public payer for long-term nursing home care for people who qualify financially, so a social work referral is appropriate. The Medigap option is tempting because Medigap “fills gaps,” but it covers Medicare cost-sharing, not services Medicare excludes.
questions.takeaway: Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care; involve social work early.
questions.hintContent: Distinguish skilled, short-term care from custodial, long-term care.
questions.hintStrategy: For “best response” items, choose the answer that is accurate and connects the family to the right resource.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A parent tells the school nurse that the family’s income is slightly too high for Medicaid and they cannot afford private insurance for their 8-year-old, who has asthma. Which program should the nurse suggest the family explore?
options: Children’s Health Insurance Program
Hospital charity care program
Supplemental Security Income program
Women, Infants, and Children program
optionRationales: Correct. CHIP insures children in families whose income is too high for Medicaid but too low to afford private coverage.
Incorrect. Charity care may lower a hospital bill, but it is not insurance and does not cover routine asthma care.
Incorrect. SSI targets low income, but it is cash aid for people with disabilities, not health insurance.
Incorrect. WIC serves low-income families, but it provides nutrition support for children under 5, not health coverage.
questions.rationale: CHIP, formerly SCHIP, uses federal and matching state funds to insure children under 19 in families whose income exceeds Medicaid limits but who cannot afford private coverage. Required benefits include routine checkups, immunizations, dental and vision care, hospital care, and lab and x-ray services, which would support this child’s asthma care. Families typically apply through the local social services department. SSI is tempting because it targets low income, but it is cash aid rather than insurance.
questions.takeaway: Children under 19 just above Medicaid income limits → CHIP.
questions.hintContent: Focus on the phrase “slightly too high for Medicaid” and the client’s age.
questions.hintStrategy: Underline the eligibility cues (age, income, status) and match them to a single program.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803–2804
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 24-year-old client with type 1 diabetes is covered by her mother’s employer plan. She tells the nurse, “I have to buy my own insurance now that I’m out of college, and no one will cover me with diabetes.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: “Insurers can charge you more because of diabetes, so stay on your mother’s plan as long as possible.”
“You must leave your mother’s plan when you graduate, but Medicaid will cover anyone with diabetes.”
“You can generally stay on your mother’s plan until age 26, and insurers cannot deny coverage for diabetes.”
“You can stay on your mother’s plan until 26, but only if you are still enrolled as a student.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. The ACA prohibits insurers from charging more because of a preexisting condition.
Incorrect. Graduation does not end dependent coverage before 26, and Medicaid eligibility depends on income and state rules, not diagnosis.
Correct. The ACA allows dependents to remain on a parent’s plan until age 26 and prohibits denial or higher charges for preexisting conditions.
Incorrect. The ACA’s age-26 provision does not require student status.
questions.rationale: The Affordable Care Act allows dependent children to remain on a parent’s plan until age 26, regardless of student status, and prohibits insurers from denying coverage or charging more because of preexisting conditions. The nurse corrects both misconceptions so the client does not risk a coverage gap that could interrupt insulin. The student-status option is tempting because many plans required it before the ACA.
questions.takeaway: ACA: dependents to age 26 and no preexisting-condition denials.
questions.hintContent: Two ACA consumer protections apply to this client.
questions.hintStrategy: Check every clause of each option; an option with one wrong clause is wrong.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2804
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A community health nurse is teaching a group about consumer protections under the Affordable Care Act. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: “Insurers cannot deny coverage because of a preexisting condition.”
“Many evidence-based preventive services are covered with no cost-sharing.”
“Plans cannot set annual dollar limits on essential health benefits.”
“Every employer, regardless of size, must provide free coverage to all employees.”
“Deductibles and co-payments are no longer allowed in any health plan.”
“Young adults can generally remain on a parent’s plan until age 26.”
optionRationales: Correct. The ACA prohibits denials and higher charges for preexisting conditions.
Correct. The ACA mandates coverage of evidence-based preventive services with zero cost-sharing.
Correct. The ACA banned annual dollar limits on essential health benefits.
Incorrect. The ACA does not require every employer to provide free coverage.
Incorrect. Cost-sharing such as deductibles and co-payments still exists; preventive services are the main zero-cost category.
Correct. Dependent children can remain on a parent’s plan until age 26.
questions.rationale: Key ACA protections include coverage expansion, a ban on annual dollar limits on essential health benefits, dependent coverage to 26, preventive services without cost-sharing, prohibition of preexisting-condition denials or surcharges, and limits on unreasonable premium increases with transparent consumer information. The ACA did not eliminate cost-sharing or require all employers to provide free coverage. Overstating protections is as harmful as understating them because clients may be surprised by bills.
questions.takeaway: ACA: no preexisting-condition denials, no annual limits on essential benefits, free preventive care, dependents to 26.
questions.hintContent: Watch for absolute words such as “every,” “free,” and “no longer allowed.”
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA teaching items, select statements that are accurate as written; overstatements are incorrect.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2804
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance

questions.stem: A client who will turn 65 next month asks which services she will need other coverage or savings to pay for if she enrolls in Original Medicare. Which services are generally not covered by Original Medicare? Select all that apply.
options: Hospice care
Long-term custodial care in a nursing home
Hearing aids
A screening mammogram
Routine dental cleanings
A walker prescribed after surgery
optionRationales: Incorrect. Part A covers hospice care.
Correct. Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care.
Correct. Hearing aids are excluded from Original Medicare.
Incorrect. Part B covers preventive screenings such as mammograms.
Correct. Routine dental care is not covered by Original Medicare.
Incorrect. Part B covers durable medical equipment such as walkers.
questions.rationale: Original Medicare Part A covers inpatient care, short-term skilled nursing facility care, hospice, and home health; Part B covers provider and outpatient services, durable medical equipment, and preventive screenings. Medicare does not cover long-term custodial care, routine dental or eye care, hearing aids, or cosmetic surgery. Clients may seek other coverage, such as Medicare Advantage plans with extras, separate dental or vision insurance, or long-term care insurance. Hospice is a common distractor because it sounds like long-term care, but it is a covered Part A benefit.
questions.takeaway: Medicare excludes long-term custodial care, routine dental and eye care, hearing aids, and cosmetic surgery.
questions.hintContent: Sort each service into Part A, Part B, or excluded.
questions.hintStrategy: For coverage SATA items, assign each option to a specific benefit before deciding.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with a PPO plan pays $40 at every specialist visit and is responsible for 20% of the hospital bill after meeting the deductible. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding of these terms?
options: “The $40 is my coinsurance, and the 20% is my co-payment.”
“The $40 is my deductible, and the 20% is my out-of-pocket maximum.”
“The $40 is my premium, and the 20% is my deductible.”
“The $40 is my co-payment, and the 20% is my coinsurance.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This reverses the terms: a fixed dollar amount is a co-payment, and a percentage is coinsurance.
Incorrect. A deductible is an annual threshold, and the out-of-pocket maximum caps total annual spending.
Incorrect. A premium is the regular payment to keep the plan active, and a deductible is paid before the plan shares costs.
Correct. A co-payment is a set dollar amount at the time of service; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost after the deductible.
questions.rationale: A co-payment is a set amount paid at the time of service, such as $40 for a specialist visit; specialist co-payments are usually higher than primary care co-payments. Coinsurance is the insured’s percentage share of a covered cost after the deductible. Premiums keep the policy active, and the out-of-pocket maximum caps total annual spending. Reversing co-payment and coinsurance is the most common error.
questions.takeaway: Co-payment = fixed dollars; coinsurance = percentage.
questions.hintContent: One term is a fixed amount and the other is a percentage.
questions.hintStrategy: When options pair two terms, verify each half of the pair independently.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2802–2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with a point-of-service (POS) plan wants knee surgery from an out-of-network orthopedic surgeon a friend recommended. What should the nurse explain about this choice?
options: “POS plans cover only emergencies outside the network, so the surgery will not be covered.”
“You may use that surgeon, but your co-payments, coinsurance, and deductible will be higher.”
“POS plans have no network, so the surgery will be covered the same as with any surgeon.”
“You must switch to a PPO plan before you can see any out-of-network provider.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. That describes an HMO; POS plans allow out-of-network care at a higher cost.
Correct. POS members decide at each point of service; out-of-network (PPO-style) care is covered with higher cost-sharing.
Incorrect. That describes an indemnity plan; POS plans have a network with lower in-network costs.
Incorrect. POS plans already include an out-of-network option; no plan change is required.
questions.rationale: A point-of-service plan is a hybrid of HMO and PPO features. Each time members seek care, they choose HMO-style in-network care, with lower cost and usually a PCP referral, or PPO-style out-of-network care with higher co-payments, coinsurance, and deductibles. The nurse should also encourage the client to check preauthorization requirements before surgery. The HMO-like distractor is tempting because POS plans share HMO features in network.
questions.takeaway: POS: choose at each visit — in network costs less, out of network costs more.
questions.hintContent: POS sits in the middle of the restrictiveness spectrum.
questions.hintStrategy: Locate the plan on the HMO-to-indemnity spectrum and eliminate options describing the plans on either side.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client with hypertension enrolled in a high-deductible consumer-driven health plan tells the clinic nurse that he stopped taking his lisinopril 2 weeks ago because he has not met his deductible. His blood pressure today is 176/102 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Teach the client how to use his health savings account to pay for prescriptions.
Notify the prescriber and ask about a lower-cost generic antihypertensive.
Assess the client for headache, chest pain, vision changes, and neurologic deficits.
Refer the client to a financial counselor to review his plan options.
optionRationales: Incorrect. HSA teaching is useful, but it does not come before assessing the client’s current physiologic status.
Incorrect. Collaboration with the prescriber is needed, but the nurse first needs focused assessment data to report.
Correct. The blood pressure is markedly elevated after stopping the medication; the nurse first assesses for symptoms of hypertensive emergency or target-organ effects.
Incorrect. Financial counseling addresses the cost barrier but is not the first priority.
questions.rationale: A blood pressure of 176/102 mm Hg after the client stopped his antihypertensive is markedly elevated. Before addressing cost, the nurse assesses for signs of hypertensive emergency or target-organ effects, such as severe headache, chest pain, dyspnea, vision changes, or neurologic changes, because findings would change the urgency of care. The nurse then reports to the prescriber, explores generic options, teaches about using HSA funds, and refers for financial counseling. Notifying the prescriber is tempting, but a report without focused assessment is incomplete.
questions.takeaway: When cost causes nonadherence, assess physiologic risk first, then solve the cost barrier.
questions.hintContent: Look at today’s blood pressure: what does the stopped medication mean for this client right now?
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before you act unless an emergency is already clear; financial solutions follow physical safety.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2802–2803
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential

questions.stem: A client being discharged after a myocardial infarction says, “I don’t know how I’ll pay for all these new prescriptions.” Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Collaborate with the prescriber about generic or formulary alternatives
Refer the client to the case manager or social worker for financial resources
Review whether the client has prescription drug coverage and what it includes
Suggest taking each medication every other day until the client can afford more
Advise the client to stop the medications that seem least important
optionRationales: Correct. Formulary and generic options can lower costs while keeping therapy appropriate.
Correct. Case managers and social workers connect clients with assistance programs and coverage.
Correct. Knowing the client’s drug coverage identifies gaps to address before discharge.
Incorrect. Changing dosing without an order is unsafe and outside the nurse’s scope.
Incorrect. Stopping cardiac medications without prescriber direction risks serious complications.
questions.rationale: Cost barriers commonly lead to nonadherence and readmission. Appropriate nursing actions are to assess coverage, collaborate with the prescriber about cost-effective formulary or generic choices, and refer to case management or social work for financial assistance. The nurse never advises altering or stopping prescribed medications without an order. Addressing affordability before discharge is part of safe discharge planning.
questions.takeaway: Address medication cost with coverage review, prescriber collaboration, and referral — never by advising dose changes.
questions.hintContent: Separate actions within the nurse’s scope from changes to the prescribed regimen.
questions.hintStrategy: In SATA items, reject any option that alters a prescription without an order.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2802–2804
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing Medicare options with a client who is enrolling in Medicare. Which statement by the client indicates a need for further teaching?
options: “I’ll buy a Medigap policy to pay the co-payments in my Medicare Advantage plan.”
“A Medicare Advantage plan bundles Parts A and B and usually includes drug coverage.”
“Part D is the part of Medicare that helps pay for my prescriptions.”
“Medigap policies help pay deductibles and coinsurance in Original Medicare.”
optionRationales: Correct. This needs correction: Medigap supplements Original Medicare and is not used with a Medicare Advantage plan.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; Part C plans bundle A and B and usually D.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; Part D provides prescription drug coverage through private plans.
Incorrect. This statement is accurate; Medigap fills Original Medicare’s cost-sharing gaps.
questions.rationale: Medicare Part C (Medicare Advantage) plans are private plans approved by Medicare that bundle Parts A and B and usually Part D. Medigap (Medicare Supplement Insurance) is private insurance that pays co-payments, coinsurance, deductibles, and gaps in Original Medicare; Medicare pays first, then Medigap. Medigap is not designed to work with Medicare Advantage, so the client’s plan would be an unnecessary expense. Students often confuse these two because both involve private insurers.
questions.takeaway: Medicare Advantage replaces Original Medicare; Medigap supplements Original Medicare.
questions.hintContent: One option is an alternative way to get Medicare; the other fills gaps in Original Medicare.
questions.hintStrategy: In “further teaching” items, look for the statement that combines two concepts that don’t go together.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 46-year-old client who began hemodialysis for end-stage renal disease 4 months ago says he lost his job and his employer insurance, and he plans to skip treatments “until I turn 65 and get Medicare.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Explain that ESRD may qualify him for Medicare now and refer him to social work today.
Urge him to keep all dialysis sessions and ask the unit about a payment plan.
Tell him that Medicare is available only to people who are 65 years of age or older.
Teach him the signs of high potassium and fluid overload that he should report.
optionRationales: Correct. ESRD can make him eligible for Medicare now; correcting the misconception and getting social work help today keeps him in treatment.
Incorrect. Keeping him in dialysis is the right goal, but a payment plan misses the Medicare coverage he likely qualifies for now.
Incorrect. Age 65 is one route, but ESRD also qualifies younger people, so this reinforces his dangerous plan.
Incorrect. Safety teaching is useful, but it accepts the plan to skip treatment rather than removing the barrier.
questions.rationale: Skipping dialysis can quickly cause life-threatening hyperkalemia and fluid overload, so the nurse’s first priority is to keep the client in treatment. Medicare is available to people 65 and older, younger people with certain disabilities, and people with ESRD or ALS, so this client likely can obtain coverage now (ESRD eligibility depends on the work history of the client or a spouse and usually begins after a short waiting period once dialysis starts). Correcting the misconception and arranging social work or case management help immediately protects the client’s safety. Telling him Medicare is only for older adults reinforces the dangerous plan.
questions.takeaway: Medicare covers ESRD and ALS regardless of age; prevent dangerous gaps in treatment.
questions.hintContent: Recall the groups younger than 65 who can qualify for Medicare.
questions.hintStrategy: Identify the physical risk (missed dialysis) and choose the action that prevents it while giving accurate information.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803

questions.stem: A client has an employer-sponsored plan with a $6,000 annual out-of-pocket maximum. By March she had paid $6,000 toward covered in-network care after a hospitalization. In June of the same plan year, she needs covered in-network outpatient surgery. What should the nurse tell her about her costs for the surgery?
options: “You will pay your deductible again because this surgery is a new episode of care.”
“You will pay 20% coinsurance again until you have paid another $6,000 this year.”
“Your plan should pay 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the plan year.”
“You will still pay your usual co-payment, but you will no longer owe any coinsurance.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Clients often think costs restart with each new episode of care, but the deductible applies once per plan year.
Incorrect. Coinsurance applies before the maximum is met, but she has already reached the annual out-of-pocket limit.
Correct. After the out-of-pocket maximum is met, the plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the plan year.
Incorrect. Co-payments usually count toward the out-of-pocket maximum, so once it is reached they also stop for covered in-network care.
questions.rationale: Employment-sponsored plans include an out-of-pocket maximum that protects against catastrophic costs. Once the insured has paid that amount for covered services within the 12-month plan period, the plan covers 100% of usual and customary fees for covered services for the rest of the period. Premiums still must be paid, and noncovered or out-of-network charges may differ, so the nurse encourages the client to confirm with her plan. The deductible-again option is tempting because clients often think costs restart with each new episode of care.
questions.takeaway: After the out-of-pocket maximum is met, covered care is paid at 100% for the rest of the plan year.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the out-of-pocket maximum is designed to protect against.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the definition of the key term exactly; eliminate options that invent resets or extra rules.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803

questions.stem: A nurse in a free clinic sees an uninsured adult with type 2 diabetes whose fingerstick glucose is 312 mg/dL. He has been out of metformin for a week and reports increased thirst but is alert with normal vital signs. He asks about health coverage. After notifying the provider about the glucose result, what should the nurse do next?
options: Tell him Medicare will cover him because he has a chronic disease.
Connect him with enrollment assistance and a social worker today.
Give him a list of pharmacies that sell low-cost generic metformin.
Advise him to apply for Marketplace coverage at the next open enrollment.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medicare covers some younger people with disabilities or ESRD, but not adults based on diabetes alone.
Correct. He is stable, so the next step is the root cause: enrollment help and social work connect him to lasting coverage and medication.
Incorrect. Low-cost generics help short term, but they do not answer his coverage question or secure ongoing care.
Incorrect. Marketplace coverage is a real option, but waiting for open enrollment delays care; Medicaid and job-loss special enrollment can start coverage sooner.
questions.rationale: The nurse first reports the elevated glucose because it requires provider evaluation; the client is alert with normal vital signs, so he is stable. The next priority is the cause of the problem: lack of coverage and medication. Enrollment assistance (for example, Medicaid if he is eligible or Marketplace coverage with subsidies) and social work referral connect him to sustainable access, and community programs may help with low-cost generics. Medicare does not cover adults based on diabetes alone, and waiting for open enrollment delays coverage he may get now.
questions.takeaway: After addressing immediate physical risk, treat lack of coverage as a care problem and refer for enrollment help.
questions.hintContent: The urgent result has been reported; consider what barrier caused it.
questions.hintStrategy: Use “next” cues: once safety is addressed, select the action that targets the root cause.

questions.stem: An uninsured client at 30 weeks’ gestation comes to a community clinic for her first prenatal visit. She says she skipped care because of cost. Her blood pressure is 152/100 mm Hg, and she reports a headache since this morning. What should the nurse do first?
options: Refer her to the local social services office to apply for Medicaid coverage.
Refer her to the WIC program for nutrition support during pregnancy.
Schedule weekly prenatal visits for the rest of her pregnancy.
Assess for visual changes, epigastric pain, and edema and notify the provider.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Medicaid enrollment is important for prenatal coverage, but it does not address the immediate risk.
Incorrect. WIC supports nutrition but is not the priority when there are signs of a hypertensive disorder.
Incorrect. Scheduling future visits does not address the current, possibly urgent finding.

Correct. Elevated blood pressure with a new headache in the third trimester suggests possible preeclampsia (headache can be a severe feature); focused assessment and prompt provider notification come first.
questions.rationale: A blood pressure of 152/100 mm Hg with a new headache at 30 weeks’ gestation suggests preeclampsia, which can progress to eclampsia or other emergencies. Physical safety comes first: assess for visual changes, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, and edema, and notify the provider promptly. After the client is evaluated, the nurse addresses the cost barrier that delayed care by referring her to Medicaid, which covers prenatal care, and to WIC. The Medicaid referral is tempting because it solves the root cause, but it does not address the immediate risk.
questions.takeaway: Treat the physical risk first; then address the coverage barrier that delayed care.
questions.hintContent: Look at the vital signs and symptoms before the insurance details.
questions.hintStrategy: When financing and clinical cues appear together, the clinical risk is usually the priority.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803

questions.stem: A nurse is screening clinic clients for possible Medicare eligibility. Which clients are most likely eligible for Medicare? Select all that apply.
options: A 67-year-old retired teacher who paid Medicare taxes for 30 years
A 40-year-old recently diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
A 45-year-old who has received Social Security disability benefits for 2 years
A 30-year-old pregnant client with a low household income
A 10-year-old whose family earns slightly more than Medicaid limits
A 58-year-old with controlled hypertension who works full time
optionRationales: Correct. People 65 and older with at least 10 years of Medicare-covered work qualify, with premium-free Part A.
Correct. People with ALS qualify for Medicare regardless of age once entitled to Social Security disability benefits, without the usual 24-month wait.
Correct. Younger people who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months qualify.
Incorrect. A low-income pregnant client would be screened for Medicaid, not Medicare.
Incorrect. This child would be screened for CHIP.
Incorrect. Age under 65 without a qualifying disability, ESRD, or ALS does not confer eligibility.
questions.rationale: Medicare covers people 65 and older (premium-free Part A after 10 years of Medicare-covered work), younger people with disabilities who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months, and people with ESRD or ALS (ALS coverage begins when disability benefits start, with no 24-month wait). Low-income pregnant clients are screened for Medicaid, and children in families just above Medicaid limits are screened for CHIP. Matching each client to the right program speeds enrollment and prevents gaps in care.
questions.takeaway: Medicare: 65+, disability after 24 months of SSDI, ESRD, or ALS; low income points to Medicaid; children above Medicaid limits point to CHIP.
questions.hintContent: Medicare eligibility is based on age, disability, or specific diagnoses — not income.
questions.hintStrategy: Classify each client into Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, or none before selecting.
questions.ref: Module 47 · Health Policy · Healthcare Financing · pp. 2803–2804
